summary: Wilde's birthday letter to Arthur Fish naming him one of his real friends — the only surviving letter between them.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote: My dear Arthur, I was charmed to get your letter, and it was delightful of you to remember my birthday. Though we see each other so rarely, I always think of you as one of my real friends, as I hope you will always think of me. Ricketts has just done for me a lovely cover for Dorian Gray - grey pastel-paper with a white back and tiny gold marigolds. When it appears I will send you a copy. How happy you must be in your little house; there are only two things in the world of any importance, Love and Art; you have both; they must never leave you. Let me send my kindest regards to your wife; I like to think that the wives of my friends are my friends also; and believe me, sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Fish, [circa 16 October 1890] - quoted whole; the editors take the text from Cassell's Weekly of 2 May 1923. Written on or about Wilde's birthday, thanking him for remembering. The Ricketts is Charles Ricketts and the cover is the 1891 Dorian Gray.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde on his own birthday naming someone one of his real friends, and what he thought the only two important things were.
